title: The whole book
hook: a year to read from the Opening to the edge of the juz' you already know
tomorrow: Seven verses, said seventeen times a day

segments.voice: Yesterday you stood at the big lookout, at the top of year one. Your line was from here you can see. What did you see when you looked back? Day three hundred thirty-two.

Pick up a printed Qur'an and open it at the front. If it's an Arabic copy, the front is on the right, because Arabic reads right to left. The first page is short: seven verses, often framed in gold. Turn it, and the second surah begins and keeps going for dozens of pages. Year one walked this book from the back, where the surahs are short enough to learn in an afternoon. Year two opens it at the front and reads forward. Today: the whole book.
screen: `OPEN IT AT THE FRONT.` → `SEVEN VERSES, FRAMED IN GOLD.` → `YEAR TWO READS FORWARD.`

segments.voice: The word Qur'an means a recitation, something read aloud. Its root, q-r-', is the same as the first command, iqra', read, that came to the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ in the cave. So the book is named for being heard. The written copy has a different name: mushaf, from a root for pages. A mushaf is the recitation, bound. Here's something that surprises people. The order of the book isn't the order the verses came down. The first verses revealed sit near the back, in Surah al-Alaq. The book opens instead with a short prayer and then the longest surah, al-Baqarah. Most Muslim scholars hold that the arrangement of the surahs, or at least of the verses within them, was set by the Prophet himself, and some say the surah order came partly from his companions. Either way, the order is old, and it's the order Muslims read in today. So this year reads that way. From al-Fatiha, the Opening, through al-Baqarah and the long Medinan surahs, through Yusuf and Maryam and the Cave, onward, until we reach the edge of the part you already walked, the thirtieth juz'. People finish the whole book all the time. In Ramadan many read one juz' a day and close the book on the last nights. Bukhari records that the Prophet told a young companion who wanted to read it all the time to take a month for each reading. We'll take a year, a few verses at a time, slow enough to hear each one. Muslims call a full reading a khatm, a sealing. This year is a long, slow khatm.
screen: `QUR'AN: A RECITATION, READ ALOUD` · `NOT THE ORDER IT CAME DOWN` · `FROM THE OPENING, ONWARD` · `A KHATM: A FULL READING, SEALED`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: choose a daily reading time. Not a big one. A slot that already exists in your day: after the dawn prayer, on the bus, with the first coffee, before you sleep. Sit now, and picture tomorrow. Where are you when you have five quiet minutes? Picture yourself there, opening the book or this app at that time. Let it become an appointment you keep. If you pray, you can say bismillah as you decide. The bell holds the time.
The whole book. A year of reading the Qur'an in order, from the Opening onward, a few verses each day, to the edge of the part you already know. Today's word.
Your line: from the opening, onward. Today, set an alarm or a note for the reading time you chose, and keep it tomorrow. Day three hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Many Muslims keep a fixed daily time for reading the Qur'an, often after the dawn prayer, and aim to complete a full reading, a khatm, over a month, a Ramadan, or longer.
